title: Vomiting, palpitations and an antiemetic

source.citation: Yamanishi Y, Iio K, Shimizu K, Kasahara W, Hamaguchi J. Metoclopramide-Induced Pheochromocytoma Crisis: A Case Report and Literature Review. Clin Case Rep. 2026;14(3):e72144.

presentation.hpi: This morning she developed palpitations and chest tightness, followed around noon by several episodes of vomiting. She has had high blood pressure and a fast heart rate for several years, treated by her primary care clinic.

exam: 10 min after IV metoclopramide 10 mg: HR 140/min, agitated, cyanotic, cold peripheries
1 h after metoclopramide: HR 170/min, RR 40/min, BP 139/113 mm Hg; SpO₂ unmeasurable because the extremities are cold
During transfer after intubation: increasing bradycardia, then loss of pulse; CPR started

imaging.finding: Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, predominantly on the left
Apical hypokinesis, ejection fraction 30%; no pericardial effusion, no D-shaped ventricle
Smooth, round left adrenal tumor, 45 mm in diameter

ecg: Monitor on arrival at the tertiary center: asystole; no shockable rhythm at any point during resuscitation

diagnosis.primary: Pheochromocytoma crisis (biochemically supported; no histology) triggered by metoclopramide, with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, pulmonary edema and cardiac arrest

management: Tracheal intubation for respiratory failure, then transfer to a tertiary center
CPR for asystolic arrest; ROSC after 20 min and 3 mg epinephrine in total
Targeted temperature management for post-cardiac arrest syndrome
Continuous phentolamine infusion titrated to blood pressure, then a landiolol infusion for tachycardia
Tumor not resected because of the poor neurological prognosis; extubated to comfort care with morphine
outcome: Severe hypoxic encephalopathy on head CT at 72 h; comfort care; died on day 18 of illness (no autopsy).
teachingPoints: Metoclopramide and other dopamine antagonists can precipitate a catecholamine crisis in undiagnosed pheochromocytoma; nausea is a presenting symptom in 20–40%.
Years of hypertension with tachycardia in a young patient, plus palpitations and chest tightness, should make you pause before giving metoclopramide.
Pheochromocytoma crisis can cause Takotsubo-type cardiomyopathy, pulmonary edema, shock and cardiac arrest; severe forms carry about 30% mortality.
Control catecholamine excess with alpha-blockade first (e.g. phentolamine) and add a beta-blocker only afterwards.
Plasma free metanephrines confirm the diagnosis (here over 50 times the upper limit); resection is curative once the patient is stable.

questions.q: What is the most likely explanation for her deterioration after the antiemetic?
options: Catecholamine crisis from an undiagnosed pheochromocytoma
questions.explanation: Within minutes of a dopamine antagonist she developed extreme tachycardia, rising diastolic pressure, peripheral vasoconstriction and respiratory failure, on a background of years of hypertension and tachycardia: a classic metoclopramide-triggered pheochromocytoma crisis. NMS evolves over days with fever and rigidity, and anaphylaxis causes vasodilatory hypotension rather than cold peripheries with hypertension.

questions.q: Which mechanism best explains the new left ventricular dysfunction?
questions.extra: After ROSC, echocardiography: apical hypokinesis, ejection fraction 30%, no pericardial effusion, no D-shaped ventricle. Chest radiograph: bilateral infiltrates.
options: Right ventricular pressure overload from pulmonary embolism
questions.explanation: A catecholamine surge causes stress (Takotsubo-type) cardiomyopathy with apical hypokinesis and pulmonary edema, which the authors describe here. No D-shaped septum argues against RV pressure overload, there is no effusion, and chronic hypertensive disease would not produce sudden apical akinesis.

questions.q: After ROSC she is hypertensive and tachycardic, with a 45 mm adrenal mass on CT. Which drug strategy is most appropriate?
options: IV esmolol first, adding an alpha-blocker only if needed
IV labetalol boluses as the only agent
IV phentolamine first, adding a beta-blocker after alpha-blockade
questions.explanation: Catecholamine excess is controlled with alpha-blockade first (phentolamine here); beta-blockade on its own leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can worsen hypertension and pulmonary edema. A beta-blocker (landiolol here) is added once alpha-blockade is in place, the 'alpha before beta' principle of the 2014 Endocrine Society pheochromocytoma guideline.

evidence.quote: A 41-year-old female patient presented to the emergency department of a secondary referral center with vomiting.
Her symptoms began with palpitations and chest tightness in the morning, followed by several episodes of vomiting around noon.
She had a history of hypertension and tachycardia of several years' duration and had been taking carvedilol and amlodipine prescribed by her primary care clinic.

evidence.field: vitals.hr, vitals.rr, vitals.spo2, vitals.sbp, vitals.dbp, vitals.tempC
evidence.quote: heart rate 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 100% on ambient air, blood pressure 133/98 mmHg, and body temperature 36.5°C
She was fully conscious at the time of her presentation.
During her evaluation, intravenous metoclopramide 10 mg was administered to alleviate her nausea.
Ten minutes later, her heart rate had risen to 140 beats per minute. She became agitated and cyanotic and exhibited peripheral coldness.
One hour after the metoclopramide administration, her heart rate reached 170 beats per minute, and her respiratory rate increased to 40 breaths per minute.
her systolic blood pressure remained unchanged at 139 mmHg, her diastolic blood pressure had risen to 113 mmHg
Her SpO2 became unmeasurable due to coldness of the extremities. She underwent tracheal intubation for respiratory failure and was transported to the study center
During transportation, the patient gradually became bradycardic, and her pulse became non-palpable, prompting the transportation team to initiate cardiopulmonary resuscitation
Upon arrival, she had cardiopulmonary arrest, with electrocardiographic monitoring showing asystole.
Shockable rhythms were not observed at any point during the resuscitation.
Spontaneous circulation was restored after 20 min of resuscitation, during which 3 mg of epinephrine in total was administered.
mixed acidosis with pH 6.99, PaCO2 65.1 mmHg, HCO3 15.5 mEq/L, and lactate 19.0 mmol/L
Severe hypoxemia was also noted, with PaO2 74.8 mmHg on 1.0 FiO2.
Chest X-ray demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, predominantly in the left lung.
Echocardiography revealed apical hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 30% indicating Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.
No pericardial effusion or D-shaped ventricular configuration was observed on echocardiography.
During ultrasonographic evaluation, a mass was incidentally detected on the left adrenal gland.
Abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a smooth, round tumor measuring 45 mm in diameter
Given that the tumor was found in the context of rapid respiratory and cardiac deterioration following the administration of metoclopramide, a pheochromocytoma crisis was strongly suspected.
Pheochromocytoma was unable to be diagnosed definitively in the present case owing to the lack of pathological information.
showing a marked elevation in the metanephrine and normetanephrine value to 52.3 nmol/L and 106.5 nmol/L, respectively
metoclopramide exacerbated the pheochromocytoma crisis in this case and led to the development of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and pulmonary edema
Intensive care, including target temperature management for post-cardiac arrest syndrome, was begun.
We initiated a continuous infusion of phentolamine mesylate and titrated the dose as needed to control hypertension.
A landiolol hydrochloride infusion was added subsequently to control tachycardia.
Head CT performed 72 h after the start of targeted temperature management found evidence of severe hypoxic encephalopathy.
Given her poor neurological prognosis, the tumor was not resected. After discussing with her family, she was extubated, and continuous morphine administration was begun
She passed away on day 18 of illness. In accordance with the family's wishes, no autopsy was performed.
